frases.t: On April 27, 2020, the Pentagon officially released three videos.
They showed objects that Navy pilots could not identify.
Their names were FLIR, GIMBAL, and GOFAST.
For years,
people said these videos proved that something unknown was flying over the ocean.
Pilots described things that moved in ways no aircraft they knew could move.
Our rule here is simple:
a case is only closed when the evidence closes it.
Today, we open the complete file: what each video shows,
what investigators found, and which case is still open.
It starts on November 14, 2004,
about 100 miles off the coast of Southern California.
A Navy cruiser, the USS Princeton, had been tracking strange radar contacts.
According to the radar operators,
some contacts seemed to drop from very high altitudes, around 80,000 feet.
Two fighter jets were sent to check one out.
One was flown by Commander David Fravor, a veteran Navy pilot.
The other was flown by Lieutenant Alex Dietrich.
When they arrived, they saw a disturbance in the water.
Above it, there was a white object,
about 40 feet long, shaped like a Tic Tac candy.
It had no wings, and no visible engines.
One of the pilots later said it
accelerated like nothing he had ever seen.
Then it was gone.
Later that day, another pilot, Chad Underwood, flew out with an infrared camera.
An infrared camera does not see light.
It sees heat.
He recorded a short video of a small object on his screen.
He was the one who first called it the Tic Tac.
That video became known as FLIR.
A copy leaked online in 2007, but for years, almost nobody paid attention.
Eleven years later, in January 2015, it happened again.
This time, over the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of Florida.
Pilots from the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt recorded two more videos.
In one, an object seems to rotate in the sky.
That one is GIMBAL.
In the other, a small object seems to race above the waves.
That one is GOFAST.
Then, on December 16, 2017,
The New York Times published a story that went around the world.
It revealed that the Pentagon had run a program to study UFO reports.
It was called the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program,
and it ran until 2012.
And it came with two of the videos: FLIR and GIMBAL.
They were released by a group co-founded by Tom DeLonge,
the guitarist of Blink-182.
A few months later, GOFAST came out too.
In 2019, the Navy confirmed the videos were real.
It also said it could not identify the objects.
The Navy even wrote new rules so pilots could report these sightings.
Then, on April 27, 2020, the Pentagon released all three videos officially.
It said it wanted to clear up
any confusion about whether the footage was real.
And its statement said the objects remain characterized as unidentified.
Now, let's open each case, one by one.
First, GOFAST.
The video makes the object look like
it is skimming the ocean at high speed.
But the screen also shows numbers:
the camera angle, the distance, and the jet's altitude.
In 2023, a NASA study team did the math.
Their conclusion: the video gives an impression of great speed,
but the numbers tell a much less extraordinary story.
The object was not near the water.
It was about 13,000 feet up.
It was moving at about 40 miles per hour,
a typical wind speed at that height.
The jet was flying at around 435 miles per hour.
That is what made the object look so fast.
It is like looking out the window of a fast car:
a slow bird can seem to race past.
And on the infrared camera, the object was colder than the ocean.
No sign of an engine.
In 2025, the Pentagon's UFO office, AARO, reached a similar answer:
about 13,000 feet up, moving with the wind.
Some researchers still argue about the exact speed.
But the idea of a craft racing over the waves is gone.
Case closed: an object drifting with the wind.
Next, GIMBAL.
In this video, the object seems to tilt and rotate,
like no normal aircraft.
Investigator Mick West argues that what rotates is not the object,
but a glare in the camera.
The camera sits on a moving mount called a gimbal.
When it turns, the glare turns with it.
Others disagree.
And even West says the video alone
does not explain everything the pilots reported.
No official report has closed this case.
So for now, GIMBAL stays in the debate pile.
Finally, the Tic Tac.
This is the hardest one.
The video itself is blurry and short.
But it is backed by something the others lack:
four aviators who say they saw the object with their own eyes.
As of today, no official report has explained it.
And the bigger picture is just as strange.
After the videos came out, Congress asked for an official report.
In 2021, US intelligence reviewed 144 reports, mostly from Navy pilots.
Only one was explained with high confidence: a large, deflating balloon.
The other 143 remained unexplained.
In 18 of them, the objects seemed to move in unusual ways.
Officials also said there was no clear sign
that any of them came from another world.
In 2022, the Pentagon created a new office to investigate these reports.
It is called AARO.
Its job is to take every case,
one by one, and look for an answer.
GOFAST is one of the cases where it published an answer.
In July 2023, David Fravor testified before Congress,
under oath, about what he saw.
Former Navy pilot Ryan Graves told the same
hearing that sightings like these were routine for pilots.
At the same hearing,
a former intelligence officer made bigger claims about hidden programs.
The Pentagon said it found no verifiable information to back those claims.
Before the final verdict,
here is a quick guide to reading any UFO video.
First, distance.
Without knowing how far away something is,
you cannot know its size or its speed.
Second, the camera.
Infrared cameras show heat,
and a hot spot can bloom into a glare that hides the real shape.
Third, motion.
When the camera itself is moving fast, slow things can look fast.
Fourth, the other evidence.
Radar, eyewitnesses, and other sensors can make a case much stronger.
That is exactly why the Tic Tac is still open:
it has more than just a video.
So here is the scorecard.
GOFAST: solved.
An object drifting with the wind.
GIMBAL: still debated.
The Tic Tac: still open.
Three videos, three different answers.
And maybe that is the real lesson:
one blurry video is never the whole story.
So next time you see a UFO video,
remember the guide: distance, camera, motion, and other evidence.
Some of these stories end with a balloon.
Some end with a camera glare.
And some, so far, do not end at all.
Tell me which case you want me to open next.
Follow The Rabbit Loop: one story leads to another.
